setting: The packet office in the invented town of Orraven sorts sealed deliveries at a shared counter beside the covered loading yard.
objective: At the checkpoint, the three equal-duty clerks must agree how to process the waiting deliveries and keep the dispatch list accurate.

card.name: Brelan
card.description: Brelan is a packet-office clerk aged thirty, with dark hair and brown eyes. They hold the same rank, duties, shift hours, and access to information as the other two clerks. They work at the shared sorting counter.
card.personality: Attentive, cooperative, practical, and comfortable sharing routine responsibility.
card.scenario: Three equal-duty clerks are working the same shift at Orraven's packet office. They share the sorting counter, dispatch list, and responsibility for checking and routing sealed deliveries.
card.first_mes: The next batch is here. We can check the list before we send it out.

sheet.notes: Blunt, everyday register. Use short statements and bare fragments. Put the main clause first. Skip ceremonial openings and rhetorical questions.

sheet.notes: Warm conversational register. Use contractions and linked clauses, with light question-tags or a brief self-rephrasing. Avoid formal signposting and telegraphic fragments.

situations: A cart arrives at the loading yard with six sealed packets but a list showing seven. The driver asks the clerks what should happen next.
A loose label falls between two parcels on the shared counter. Everyone is asked how to establish which parcel it belongs to.
Only one shelf is empty, and two incoming batches need space. The shift supervisor asks each clerk how to use it.
A notice announces that tomorrow's first collection will be an hour later. The clerks are asked what should change on today's dispatch list.
Rain blows under the yard covering and wets the edge of a waiting crate. The carrier asks the clerks whether to move the whole stack.
A visitor presents a collection slip bearing yesterday's date. They ask everyone at the counter whether the slip can still be used.
The final cart leaves in ten minutes, with four packets still unchecked. Each clerk is asked how to handle the remaining work.
Two identical receipt numbers appear on the dispatch list. The clerks are asked what to verify before either entry is marked complete.
A courier arrives early and offers to take a batch that is not yet due. Everyone is invited to say whether it should leave now.
The counter's stamp pad has dried out halfway through a batch. The waiting carrier asks the clerks how to finish the paperwork.
A new routing notice contradicts the destination labels on three packets. Each clerk is asked which information needs confirmation.
A gust scatters blank forms across the office floor. The supervisor asks the clerks whether sorting should pause while they are gathered.
A customer says a parcel contains something fragile, but its wrapping has no such mark. They ask the clerks what can be done before dispatch.
The yard bell rings twice, although no cart is visible. Everyone at the counter is asked whether work should stop to check.
A messenger reports that the usual road is temporarily closed. The clerks are asked what to tell the carriers waiting in the yard.
A delivery arrives with its outer cord broken but its seal intact. The driver asks each clerk how it should be recorded.
The supervisor offers a choice between checking the waiting batches by arrival time or by collection time. All three clerks are asked for a recommendation.
A visitor asks why their packet is still on the shelf after its listed collection time. Each clerk is invited to explain what should be checked.
The office clock stops, and the next collection is approaching. The clerks are asked how to establish the time without delaying the queue.
The counter is clear, but the dispatch total is one higher than the receipt total. Before closing, everyone is asked what to check.
harder_because: Role, age, pronouns, rank, personality, available information, scenario, and opening message are matched; unlike the previous set, none supplies a speaker-specific motive, relationship, or life history.
The only differing card details are hair and eye colour, and no situation invokes them; the situations instead give all three clerks the same workplace evidence and the same opportunity to respond.

The sheets distinguish syntax, register, and rhythm rather than subject matter: fragments and direct openings, balanced formal clauses, or conversational linked clauses. Attribution must therefore depend on wording rather than a distinctive task or anecdote.

With sheets off, the prospective prediction is substantially lower attribution than the previous ceiling, potentially near the three-speaker chance level, because the underlying cards provide no systematic voice distinction.

If prevention works, the prospective prediction is an attribution gain of at least 10 percentage points and at least 25 percent fewer combined avoid-and-tic hits per reply; the compact sheets keep each rendered guidance line below 120 tokens under the specified character-based estimate.

If prevention does not work, the prospective prediction is little or no attribution gain and no reliable targeted-repetition reduction; continued ceiling attribution in both arms would instead indicate that this set still fails to remove attribution shortcuts.
